name: Web egress guardrails for fetch and browser (LAN, SSRF, blocklists)
description: Makes sure nothing Happy fetches or browses can reach the home network (Hue bridge, printer, router page) or carry a secret along, and records which protections are hard limits and which are best effort. Every other web feature in this lens sits on top of it.
example: Trigger: an injected page tells the research agent to open the router's admin page; the call is refused before a request is sent, and the nightly eval has a case for it.
how: Gateway config, applies to the research agent. Keep `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` unset (strict is the default). Add known paste and tracker hosts to `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames`. Leave `tools.web.fetch.headers` empty, because the model picks the URL and any header goes wherever it points. Leave `tools.web.fetch.provider` unset and do not install a fetch-provider plugin, so a failed fetch is never retried through a third party. Set `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Second layer if the roadmap's egress proxy is built: `proxy.proxyUrl` for the gateway's own HTTP clients. Add two eval cases to the M3 exit test: a LAN address, and a public URL that redirects to one.
caveats: web_fetch blocks private hosts and re-checks redirects. The browser's check is weaker: the docs say its request interception is not a network firewall and can miss redirect hops, a popup's first request and Service Worker traffic.

The managed browser does not inherit the gateway's proxy environment, and strict SSRF mode blocks an explicit browser proxy flag unless private-network access is switched on. Putting the browser behind the roadmap's filtering proxy is therefore an open design conflict to settle before M3.
OpenClaw does not ship or run a proxy; `proxy.proxyUrl` only routes its own HTTP and WebSocket clients through one you operate.
There is no public-web allowlist setting: `allowedHostnames` only re-opens individual private hosts and `blockedHostnames` only denies. A per-agent site allowlist has to be a hook (WEB-03).
safety: Takes the home LAN out of reach of any agent that reads untrusted pages. It does not stop an injected page from making the agent request some public URL; that is contained by the research agent holding no private data and no accounts.
unverified: The roadmap's plan to drop LAN access inside the Colima VM would not cover a browser that runs on the host; this follows from where the process runs and was not tested.
Which hosts belong on the blocklist is a judgment call, not something the docs prescribe.

name: Logged-out rendering browser for the research agent (read-only)
description: Lets research read pages that plain fetch cannot: script-rendered calendars, town 'what goes where' widgets, rec-department listings. Logged out, no typing, nothing clicked beyond following a link. New versus F020: a sourced comparison of the three places a browser can live, and a read-only action set enforced in code.
example: "What time does the town pool open on Saturday? Their site is one of those app-style pages."
how: Holder: `research` (stateless, memory off, no accounts). `agents.entries.research.tools.alsoAllow: ["browser"]`; a dedicated managed profile (for example `browser.profiles.research` with its own `cdpPort` and `headless: true`). Because sandbox mode is `all`, research's browser calls default to the sandbox target, so either set `agents.entries.research.sandbox.browser.allowHostControl: true` and use the host-managed profile, or build the sandbox browser image. `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. The WEB-03 hook allows research only `status`, `tabs`, `open`, `navigate`, `snapshot`, `text`, `screenshot`, `close` and blocks `act`, `upload`, `download`, `dialog`, `importprofile`. Placement comparison: (1) host-managed profile: own user data directory, works headless, least bot-detection trouble, but runs on the host so container network rules do not cover it; (2) sandbox browser container: strongest isolation, but the image is not in the npm package, it cannot run with network `none`, and the docs say it trips bot detection more often; (3) the `user` and `chrome` profiles attach to a real signed-in Chrome and are wrong for research (WEB-05).
depends_on: Google Chrome launchable from the happy account
caveats: Anti-bot walls, CAPTCHAs and MFA still stop it. The bundled browser skill tells the agent to stop and report the blocker, and that is the behaviour to keep.
`allowHostControl: true` lets a sandboxed agent drive a host browser; the docs say to leave it off unless the agent is trusted, so the profile pin in WEB-03 is a precondition, not a nicety.
A page snapshot costs far more tokens than a fetch; use it only after web_fetch comes back empty.
For a one-off look, opening the link on the phone is quicker.
Independent testing on live sites finds web agents markedly less reliable than benchmark numbers suggest; keep tasks to 'open one page and read it'.
safety:
Research holds no private data, and as a sub-agent it cannot hold the `message` tool, so two trifecta legs are missing by construction. Read-only actions remove form submission as a way out; navigating to a URL remains one, which is acceptable only because nothing private is in its context. Task text from

-main must stay free of names, school and address (F019 handoff rule).
unverified: Whether the happy account can launch headless Chrome under launchd without a logged-in desktop session on this Mac.

No per-agent browser-profile allowlist was found in the installed docs; the tool source contains a run-bound tab binding that pins profile and tab for a run, but whether an operator can set it per agent is not documented in what was read.

name: Browser action firewall hook (profile pin, site allowlist, approval before typing, no submit)
description: One in-house plugin that decides in code what each agent's browser may do: which profile, which sites, which actions, and which actions need a parent's yes first. Without it the browser tool is all-or-nothing, so every logged-in or form idea in this lens depends on it.
example: Trigger: an agent tries to type into a web form; the asking parent gets a text with the site and field count and an `/approve <id> allow-once` line, and the call is blocked if nobody answers within ten minutes.
how: Plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`. It reads `ctx.agentId` and `event.params` (`action`, `kind`, `profile`, `target`, `url`, `submit`, `key`). Rules per agent, all failing closed: reject any `profile` or `target` other than the one assigned; allow `open`/`navigate` only to an exact hostname list; allow only a listed subset of the tool's 24 actions; return `block: true` for act kinds `evaluate` and `press`, and for `type` with `submit`; return `requireApproval` with `allowedDecisions: ["allow-once", "deny"]` for `fill`, `type`, `select`, `click`, `upload`. Unknown agent, missing field or parse error returns a block. Prompts are answered in the same chat that raised them with a typed `/approve <id> <decision>`; `approvals.plugin.enabled` adds native iMessage delivery. Lobster is not the gate here: it is disabled in sandboxed contexts.
depends_on: approval prompts routed to the asking chat
caveats: The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. The safe rule is an approval on every click inside a form, which becomes tedious after three prompts.
Approval waits are capped at ten minutes and an unanswered request denies.
Scheduled runs have no approval route, so approval-gated actions never happen unattended. That is the intended behaviour.

On iMessage the approver list is the channel allowlist, not the requester: the roadmap already notes that approvals are not tied to the person whose agent asked, so prompts must go only to the asking chat.
A navigation allowlist in a hook checks the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next.
safety: This is what turns 'the model was told not to' into a limit the model cannot argue past: profile, site and action limits live in code and fail closed, in line with both vendors' guidance to restrict sites and confirm consequential actions. It does not by itself make a logged-in browser safe (see WEB-04).
unverified: Whether an approval raised by a spawned sub-agent is delivered to the parent chat that started the task; needs a test.
Whether tapback approval works in iMessage Basic mode; the typed /approve command is the documented fallback.
The parameter names were read from the browser tool's schema source, not observed in a live hook event.

name: Read-only portal agent on a dedicated logged-in profile
description: For the few questions only a logged-in page can answer on demand ("what is checked out on the kids' library cards?"): a per-parent, memory-less agent opens one allowlisted portal in a browser profile the parent signed in to by hand, reads one page, and returns a short structured answer. It never types, pays or changes a setting. Start with one low-stakes portal and expect upkeep.
example: "What's still checked out on the library cards, and when is it due?"
how:
Holder: `

-portal`, one per adult, because accounts are per person and shared agents hold none. Memory off, session-scoped sandbox, tools `browser` only: no web_search, no web_fetch, and as a sub-agent it cannot have `message`. Profile: `browser.profiles.portal-

` (managed, own user data directory and `cdpPort`), with the browser's password manager and sync turned off. Login: the parent signs in by hand in that profile; the operator opens it with `openclaw browser --browser-profile portal-

open ` and the parent uses Screen Sharing to the Mac mini. The agent is never given a password. WEB-03 hook: profile pinned, hostnames limited to that one portal, actions limited to `open`, `navigate`, `snapshot`, `text`, `close`.

-main reaches it through `sessions_spawn` with `subagents.allowAgents`, and the answer returns as `llm-task` JSON (titles, dates, numbers). Excluded by rule: lunch-payment portals, banks, health portals, any page with a pay button.
depends_on: Tony's decision to keep any site login on the Mac mini
Screen Sharing into the happy session for manual login
caveats: Sessions expire and many portals re-ask for MFA. Expect 'needs login' texts and a hands-on re-login every few weeks; the agent must stop there and not retry.
Most of what these portals show is already emailed by the service (WEB-07, WEB-08, WEB-09), which needs no browser at all.
A logged-in profile is the account. The docs say to treat it as sensitive state, and any agent that holds the browser tool and knows the profile name can use it unless a hook says otherwise.
The portal's own phone app answers the same question in two taps.
The vendors' own consumer browser agents add live supervision on logged-in sites or block whole site categories; an unattended family build has neither safeguard.
safety: All three trifecta legs meet in one agent: account data, page content, and navigation as a way out. It is defensible only with the way-out leg cut hard: one hostname, read-only actions, no message tool, no memory, schema-validated return. The hostname rule is a hook and the docs say the browser's request interception is not a firewall, so a residual leak path remains until the browser sits behind an egress proxy. No payments, no settings changes, no CAPTCHA solving. Recommendation: defer until WEB-03 has been tested against the injection suite.
unverified: Whether a managed profile keeps its login across gateway restarts and Chrome updates on this Mac.
Which of the family's portals keep a session without MFA on each visit.
Individual portals' terms of use may forbid automated access; not checked per site.

name: Driving a parent's real signed-in Chrome (attach, extension relay, cookie copy)
description: OpenClaw can reach a real signed-in Chrome three ways: the `user` profile (DevTools attach), the `chrome` profile (browser extension relay), and copying cookies into a managed profile. For this family all three are the wrong tool: they hand an agent a parent's whole logged-in life, and they do not fit a gateway that runs in its own macOS account on a headless Mac mini. Recorded so the answer is on file.
example: "Can Happy just use my Chrome, where I'm already logged in to everything?" Answer: no, and here is why.
how: Documented mechanisms. `user`: attaches through Chrome DevTools MCP to a running Chrome 144 or newer with remote debugging switched on; Chrome shows an Allow prompt, so someone must be at that computer. `chrome`: the OpenClaw extension uses `chrome.debugger` and works with nobody at the desk, but needs OpenClaw or a paired browser node on the same machine as that Chrome, and fresh pairings expose all tabs. Cookie copy: `openclaw browser import-profile` reads a Chrome profile on the same host after a Keychain prompt; `cookie-sync --domains` pushes live session cookies from another Mac. Guards to set instead: `browser.allowSystemProfileImport: false`, `gateway.nodes.browser.mode: "off"`, never `browser.defaultProfile: "user"` or `"chrome"`, and the WEB-03 hook rejecting those profile names. Holder: none.
caveats: The parents' Chrome sessions live on their own Macs and phones, not in the happy account. Reaching them means pairing a parent's computer as a node, which the docs say to treat like admin access.
The docs say attaching to an existing session is not safer: the agent can act as the user wherever that Chrome is signed in (mail, bank, school).
Chrome's own documentation for agent auto-connect says the agent gets everything in the profile, cookies included.
Copied cookies are live credentials sitting in a second place, the import is on by default, and device-bound sessions can refuse to work after a copy.
If one portal login is ever needed, a fresh manual login in a dedicated profile (WEB-04) is narrower than any of these.
safety: Cannot respect the trifecta: a real Chrome profile is private data, the open web is untrusted content, and the same browser is the way out. It also breaks 'one agent per person and permission set', since a browser profile is not scoped to one account. A decision record with config guards, not a build item.
unverified: Whether Chrome on macOS 27 enforces device-bound sessions; the Chrome page read does not list platforms.
The `gateway.nodes.browser.mode` value was read in the docs, not checked against the family's current config.

name: Registration pre-fill that stops before submit (camp, activities)
description: Happy could type a child's details into a camp or activity registration form and stop before the last button. Honest verdict: do not build the browser part. Build the cheap substitute instead: a registration-day card (direct link, opening time, the answers as a copy-paste block, a reminder ten minutes before) and let the phone's autofill do the typing.
example: "Camp sign-up opens Tuesday at 9. Get everything ready so I just have to tap through."
how:
Recommended path, mostly on the stack now:

-main builds the copy-paste block from vault facts (F067); research confirms the opening time and the direct link with web_fetch (F026, F029); `automations` sets the reminder (F007); the parent fills the form with browser autofill and submits. Not-recommended path, for the record: a `

-forms` agent with `browser` on a managed profile, the WEB-03 hook with an exact registration-host allowlist, `fill` and `select` behind `requireApproval`, `type` with `submit` and `press` blocked, and the parent finishing over Screen Sharing.
caveats: The form ends in a booking and usually a payment, both on the never list, so the agent would stop exactly where the time pressure is.
The browser lives on the Mac mini in the happy account. 'Finish it yourself' means Screen Sharing into that session from a phone, which is slower than filling the form on the phone.
A large registration platform's terms forbid robots and automated registration processing; expect waiting rooms and bot checks on popular sign-ups.

The form needs a child's name, birth date, health notes and emergency contacts. An agent that holds those and reads an arbitrary web page has all three trifecta legs, and vendor guidance treats typing sensitive data into a form as transmitting it.
Web agents are measurably unreliable on live sites; a mis-click on a timed registration costs the slot.
Browser autofill already stores names, addresses and contact details and fills them in one tap.
safety:
The recommended path keeps child data in

-main (no browser) and public lookups in research (no child data); no agent types anything into a third-party site. The not-recommended path cannot break the trifecta and touches the never list at its last step.

Whether any of those platforms offer a saved-family-profile feature that makes pre-fill moot.

name: School lunch balance: the service's own low-balance email, not the portal
description: "Lunch money is running low" as one line in the afternoon school digest, with no portal login anywhere. The lunch payment service sends the email itself once a parent switches the alert on; Happy only reads it. Adds to F056 the vendor-documented mechanism and the one-time setup step.
example: Trigger: the lunch service emails that a student's balance fell below the chosen amount; the 16:00 digest carries "Lunch balance low (younger child). Top up in the app."
how: Mechanism choice: an email already sent by the service. One-time parent step in the lunch portal: enable the low-balance email for each student and set the amount; then add a mail rule forwarding those messages to the school mailbox (F051). Reader: the tool-less, memory-less `school-mail` agent with the sender on its allowlist; the line is rendered by the F056 digest job. No web_fetch, no browser, no API. Topping up stays with the parent.
depends_on: a parent enables the alert in the lunch portal
caveats: You hear about it only when the balance crosses the threshold. "What is the balance right now" needs a login and belongs to the parent's app.
One vendor documents a small fixed number of emails per low-balance episode, so a broken forwarding rule means silence. Test the rule once with a high threshold.
Balance pages sit next to stored payment methods, so a logged-in browser on this portal is not recommended even read-only (WEB-04 exclusion).
The service's app can already notify the phone; the gain is one digest instead of another app to check.
safety: The reader has no tools and no memory; the email is untrusted content but there is nothing to act with. Links are relayed only when they match the sender's domain (F056 rule). No payment action exists anywhere in the flow, which keeps the never list intact.
unverified: Which lunch payment system the district uses and whether it offers the same alert; the cited service is one example.
No parent-facing balance API was found for the cited service; absence is not proven.

name: Library due dates and holds: notice emails first, account page only on request
description: Due-soon and hold-ready notices for every family library card folded into the daily digest, using the emails the library already sends. A full "what is checked out" list on demand is the one library question that needs a login, and it is the natural first (and maybe only) use of WEB-04.
example: "Anything due at the library this week?" or trigger: a hold-ready email arrives.
how: Mechanism choice: service email. Set every card's notification preference to email (parents' and kids' cards) and forward those notices to the household or school mailbox (F051). The tool-less reader extracts title, due date and pickup-by date for the digest (F056) and offers a day-before reminder (F007). Library events: subscribe the library's calendar feed if it has one (G012). Full list on demand: WEB-04 with the library as the single allowlisted host. Plain web_fetch is not an option because account pages need a login. Renewing and placing holds stay with the parent.
depends_on: WEB-04 only for the on-demand list
caveats: Notices cover what is about to be due, not the whole shelf; the full list needs the login path.
The example library notes that a third-party reminder service that worked from patron accounts is being discontinued: tools built on library accounts from the outside are fragile.
Each card usually has one email address; a parent has to set the kids' cards up once.
The library's own app shows all of this already.
safety: Tool-less reader, no memory. Titles on a child's card are low-sensitivity but still never go to research. The agent places no holds and renews nothing; state-changing clicks stay human.
unverified: Which catalog system the family's library uses, when it sends notices, and whether it offers a patron feed or API.
Whether the library auto-renews, which changes how useful a due-date reminder is.

name: Utility bills and usage, read-only: bill emails plus a Green Button file
description: "The electric bill is ready, due on the 14th" from the utility's own email, and an occasional deeper look at usage from a standard data file a parent downloads. No agent logs in to a utility account.
example: "Why was the electric bill so high last month?"
how:
Mechanism choice: service email for bills (amount when shown, due date) through the mail reader: the household mailbox before M4, the bill-nudge leg of F060 after. Official data file for usage: where the utility offers Green Button download, a parent downloads the file from the utility portal and sends it to Happy, and

-main summarises month-over-month use. The automated Green Button variant is a channel for third parties the customer authorises with the utility, not something a home agent can simply switch on. Browser session in the utility portal: not built, because payment methods and autopay live there.
depends_on: F051 mailbox or M4 mail reader
caveats: The download still requires the customer to log in to the utility portal; that step stays with the parent.
Many bill emails say only that a bill is ready, with the amount behind the login; then Happy can relay the due date and nothing more.
Autopay and the utility's own app already cover the reminder; the only new value is the comparison across months.
Do not push usage data through `code_execution` for charts: that tool runs on xAI's servers.
safety:
Bill emails are private data read by a tool-less reader with no way out. The usage file goes to

-main, which has no browser and no fetch. No payment, no autopay changes, no portal session.
unverified: Whether the family's electric, gas and water utilities offer Green Button or put amounts in their bill emails.
Whether a Green Button XML file sent over iMessage reaches the model as readable text; not checked.

name: Town recycling pages and public page watchers: feed first, fetch second, browser last
description: Bin days, holiday shifts and "does this go in recycling?" answered from the town's own published schedule, and "tell me when this public page changes" watchers, each on the least powerful mechanism that works. New versus F029, F038 and G012: a sourced order of preference, and the rule that a watcher never runs on a logged-in profile.
example: "Is recycling delayed this week because of the holiday?" or "Tell me when the rec department posts the summer swim schedule."
how: Order of preference. (1) Official feed or reminder: some municipal collection tools export the schedule to standard calendar formats and send their own reminders (example cited); subscribe the feed in the family calendar (G012) and let the town do the weekly nudge. Pages with RSS or Atom go through the `blogwatcher` CLI as a host command job (`--command-argv`, no model call). (2) `web_fetch` by research for a static schedule page, refreshed yearly into home-store (F038). (3) Watcher: `automations add --every 6h --trigger-script`, owned by research, where the script fetches the page and compares a hash or phrase with `trigger.state` (F029). (4) The logged-out browser (WEB-02) only when the page is a script-driven widget. Never: a watcher on a logged-in profile.
caveats: Each watcher check gets 30 seconds and five tool calls and runs with the owning agent's whole tool policy, so the owner has to be research (no exec).
A watcher that fails quietly looks healthy; alert on fetch failure as well as on change.
Address-lookup collection widgets are script apps, so plain fetch returns an empty shell; the calendar export is the practical route.
The town's own reminder does the weekly nudge better than Happy can. Happy adds the holiday-shift answer and the calendar entry.
`blogwatcher` is a Go-installed CLI and is not on this Mac yet.
safety: Public data only, read by research (no memory, no accounts) or by a host job with no model in the loop. A watcher's message to the owner is short and fixed-form; page text is not relayed verbatim, which limits what an edited page can say to a parent.
unverified: Whether the family's town publishes a calendar feed or uses a collection-schedule vendor; the cited city page is an example of the pattern.
Whether the calendar export on such tools is a live subscription or a one-time download.

name: Recipe link to ingredients and steps
description: Text a recipe link and get the ingredient list and the steps without the life story and the ads, scaled to the number of people, with an offer to add what is missing to the grocery list.
example: "<recipe link> What do I need for this for six people?"
how:
Mechanism choice: plain `web_fetch`, which reduces a page to its main content; schema.org also defines a Recipe vocabulary (`recipeIngredient`, `recipeInstructions`, `recipeYield`) that recipe sites can embed.

-main hands the URL to research with `sessions_spawn`; research fetches and returns JSON checked by `llm-task` against a small schema (title, yield, ingredients[], steps[], source URL, fetched-at);

-main scales quantities and proposes list items (F032), written only after a yes. Fallbacks in order: WEB-02 `text` action for script-rendered pages; a host-side `summarize --extract` wrapper for video recipes.
caveats: The fetch returns the readable article text. It is not documented to return the page's embedded Recipe data, so the model parses ingredients from prose and can drop a line. Always include the source link.
Some recipe sites sit behind bot walls or paywalls and return nothing; say so instead of guessing.
The phone's reader view and recipe-keeper apps already do the clean-up; the added value is the hand-off to the shared grocery list.
Scaling quantities is arithmetic done by a language model: fine for a stew, worth a second look for baking.
safety:
The untrusted page is read by research only. What crosses to

-main is schema-validated strings, which bounds what an injected page can pass along. List writes need the parent's yes. Nothing private goes to research: a URL and a serving count.
unverified: Whether web_fetch output ever includes a page's JSON-LD blocks; not tested.
How many of the recipe sites this family uses embed schema.org Recipe data.

name: Save a public page as a PDF (and why receipts are a mail job)
description: "Save this page as a PDF" for a public page such as a camp packing list or a recall notice, so it can be printed at home or filed. Receipts are a different case: the order email is the receipt and the mail reader already has it.
example: "Save the camp packing-list page as a PDF and print two copies."
how: Mechanism: the managed browser's `pdf` action, run by research in the logged-out profile (WEB-02 with `pdf` added to its allowed actions). The file lands in OpenClaw's temp root on the host. It is only useful as the front half of 'print it' (the F080 print plugin takes the path) or of the document vault (F044). When the link is already a PDF, the print plugin downloads it itself; the `pdf` tool only analyses documents. Receipts: mechanism choice is the service's email, forwarded as it is.
depends_on: F080 print plugin or F044 vault as the consumer
caveats: On the phone, Share then Print or Save to Files makes the same PDF in two taps. This is worth building only when the next step is the home printer.
PDF export and download interception do not work on existing-session (real Chrome) profiles.
Moving a file from research's browser output to the print plugin or to another agent is in-house plumbing; nothing in the docs read does it for you.
The `pdf` analysis tool rejects http(s) links when it runs sandboxed, so 'read this PDF link' has to go another way.
The bundled `nano-pdf` skill edits PDFs through an outside model and has no role here.
safety: Logged-out public pages only. A logged-in "save my order receipt" would need WEB-04 on a shopping account and is not built. Browser outputs are untrusted input and stay in the temp root until the print plugin's own checks.
unverified: Whether the `message` tool can attach a file from the browser temp root in iMessage Basic mode without widening the attachment roots.
Whether a hook can leave `pdf` enabled while blocking `download` for the same agent; they are separate actions in the schema, so it should.

name: Store stock check
description: "Does the store near us have this in stock?" Honest answer most of the time: Happy cannot verify it and should hand back the product link and the store's phone number. A few retailers publish an official availability API; for the rest, store pages sit behind bot detection. Adds to F026 the official-API route and the reason stealth is off the table.
example: "Is the 24-inch kids' bike in stock at a store near us today?"
how: Order: (1) an official API where one exists, wrapped as a host-side tool for research with the home area pinned server-side (one electronics retailer documents per-product store availability by postal code with an API key); (2) `web_fetch` of the product page, expecting a bot wall; (3) the logged-out browser (WEB-02), which sometimes works and is often challenged; (4) answer "could not verify" with the link. Not used: stealth proxies or hosted stealth browsers (WEB-14). No cart, no reserve, no pickup order.
caveats: Bot-management products are built to flag headless browsers, so the browser route is unreliable on large retail sites.
The retailer's own app, set to the family's store, is faster and more accurate.
One API integration per retailer is real upkeep for a question asked a few times a year.
The bundled `ordercli` skill covers one European food-delivery service and has no use here.
safety: Public data, research agent, no accounts. The home postal code is pinned inside the host tool, not passed in task text. Purchases and reservations are on the never list.
unverified: Whether the general retailers this family uses offer any public stock API; none was found in this run.
How often the logged-out browser gets through on specific retail sites; not tested.
How closely retailers' online stock flags track the shelf; a phone call is the safer check.

name: Bot-wall workarounds: stealth proxies, hosted browsers, CAPTCHA solving
description: OpenClaw documents ways past sites that block automation: a third-party fetch fallback with a stealth proxy mode, and hosted browsers with built-in CAPTCHA solving and residential proxies. They would make stock checks and some portals 'work'. For this family they stay off, and Happy reports the block instead.
example: "That site blocked Happy. Can we make it get through anyway?" Answer: no; Happy says what blocked it and gives the link.
how: A decision record plus two config guards: leave `tools.web.fetch.provider` unset and do not install `@openclaw/firecrawl-plugin` (once selected, its fetch fallback works without a key); add no remote CDP profile for a hosted browser. Agent instructions for research and any portal agent: on a login wall, CAPTCHA, MFA prompt or a 403, stop and report the exact blocker, which is what the bundled browser skill already tells the agent to do.
caveats: CAPTCHA solving is on the family's never list, and a model vendor's own browser agent is barred from bypassing captchas.
A hosted browser or fetch proxy sees every URL and page: a new third party for family traffic.
The docs warn that automated logins trip anti-bot defenses and can lock the account; a locked school or library account costs more than any feature here is worth.
Getting around a site's bot controls can breach its terms of use.
The price of saying no: stock checks and some rec-department pages will come back as 'could not verify'.
safety: Keeps the never list intact (CAPTCHA solving) and keeps page content and URLs from flowing to an extra provider. The stop-and-report behaviour is an instruction, so the hard part is done by absence: no stealth provider is installed for the model to call.
unverified: The data-retention terms of the fetch-proxy and hosted-browser vendors were not read in this run.
